# Novelty and no analogue futures {#sec-novelty}

## Background {#sec-background}

The modern analogue technique (MAT) is a standard approach for making quantitative inferences about past vegetation and climate from fossil pollen data, and from many other forms of palaeoecological data [@chevalier2020; @williams2008; @gavin2003; @overpeck1985]. The MAT relies on reasoning by analogy [@jackson2004], in which it is assumed that two compositionally similar pollen assemblages were produced by similar plant communities, growing under similar environments. The similarity of pollen assemblages is determined by the calculation of dissimilarity metrics.

The MAT can also be thought of as a non-parametric statistical technique, that computer scientists call a $k$-nearest neighbours algorithm. It is a simple form of machine learning. Each fossil pollen assemblage is matched to 1 or more ($k$) modern pollen assemblages, then is assigned the ecological and environmental characteristics associated with those modern analogues. 

The MAT is a popular approach for reconstructing past environments and climates, due to its relative simplicity and intuitive appeal. However, like any algorithm, if used unwisely, it can produce spurious results. More generally, when reasoning by analogy, be careful! Analogies are always incomplete and imperfect, and you must use your critical judgement to determine whether these imperfections are minor or serious.

To reconstruct past environments using the MAT, we need three data sets:

1. Modern species assemblages.

2. Modern environmental variables.

3. Fossil species assemblages.

The MAT follows four basic steps:

1. Calculate dissimilarities between a fossil species assemblage $i$ and all modern species assemblages in set $S$.

2. Discard modern samples with dissimilarities greater than a threshold.

3. Identify and retain the $k$ closest modern analogues.

4. Average the environmental conditions associated with the modern analogues and assign them to fossil sample $i$.

Note that we are taking a detour into palaeoclimatology for two reasons. First, because palaeoclimatic reconstructions are still a primary use for fossil pollen and other micropalaeontological data. Second, because the MAT and the `analogue` package, as a dissimilarity-based approach, also lets us explore the novelty of past communities, perhaps of more interest to palaeoecologists than inferred palaeoclimates!

The following section, @sec-datawrangle, takes you through some pretty advanced data wrangling required to match species names between the datasets we will use. However, if you prefer to skip all the wrangling and jump directly to the analyses in @sec-crossvalid, the data have been saved post-wrangling and can be loaded into R directly. Run the 'Jump point' code below and portal to @sec-crossvalid.

::: {.callout-tip}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(dplyr, tidyr, readr, tibble, stringr, neotoma2, analogue)
```

## Data wrangling {#sec-datawrangle}

In this case, data are coming from two separate sources, NeotomaDB and the North American Modern Pollen Dataset (NAMPD). We will use the NAMPD [@whitmore2005] for the cross-validation analysis. Note that the NAMPD is pre-loaded into the `analogue` package, but here we’ll use the original (more complete) data so that we can filter locations easily. Some of the data wrangling required to get two matrices containing the same species with identical names for the correct region (as required by the MAT function) is fairly advanced. This type of wrangling is quite common in palaeoecological data-science as you may be dealing with, for example, raw data collected by individuals, or from different databases that are stored in inconsistent formats.

Ready to wrangle? Let’s get the data ready:

::: {.callout-tip}
# Respawn code

The following code (unfold by clicking the dropdown) downloads the data from the neotoma API and formats it with basic harmonisation and pollen proportions calculated. This part of the data wrangling is covered in detail in @sec-neotoma2 so, more easily, you can read in the pre-wrangled .rds file from the data directory. Note that this is the long format data _not_ the species only matrix from the jump point above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# The following code can be done in one pipeline but we have split it into chunks to help with readability
devils_samples <- get_sites(siteid = 666) %>% # Download the site samples data
  get_downloads() %>%
  samples()

devils_samples <- devils_samples %>%
  dplyr::filter(ecologicalgroup %in% c("UPHE", "TRSH"), # Filter ecological groups by upland heath and trees and shrubs
                elementtype == "pollen", # filter bu pollen samples
                units == "NISP") %>% # Filter by sampling unit
         mutate(variablename = replace(variablename,
                                stringr::str_detect(variablename, "Pinus.*"), # Harmonize Pinus into one group
                                "Pinus"),
                variablename = replace(variablename,
                                stringr::str_detect(variablename, "Ambrosia.*"),
                                "Ambrosia")) %>%
  group_by(siteid, sitename,
           sampleid, variablename, units, age,
           agetype, depth, datasetid,
           long, lat) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups='keep') # The group_by function will drop columns not used as grouping variables

devils_samples <- devils_samples %>% # Calculate proportions of each species by year group
  group_by(age) %>%
  mutate(pollencount = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(variablename) %>%
  mutate(prop = value / pollencount) %>%
  arrange(desc(age)) %>%
  ungroup()

# saveRDS(devils_samples, "./data/devils_samples.rds") # Save the data for later
```
:::


:::

To read in the pre-wrangled long data for Devil's Lake use:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Load up the data
devils_samples <- readRDS("./data/devils_samples.rds")
```
:::


We will use the North American Modern Pollen Database (NAMPD) to create modern analogues [@whitmore2005]. The NAMPD includes both modern surface pollen samples and climate measurements. It is not (yet) accessible through Neotoma, but a copy is saved in the data directory of this book, so we can read it from there. It is always good to keep your own copy of data you depend on: servers are not maintained forever, and datasets are sometimes revised or withdrawn. The original is distributed as an Excel workbook; we have saved the two sheets we need as CSV, which is a plainer format that also shows up properly in version control.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_pol  <- read_csv("./data/nampd-pollen.csv",  show_col_types = FALSE)
mod_clim <- read_csv("./data/nampd-climate.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```
:::


Still with me? Great! Now we have our three datasets:

1. Our site of interest (Devil's Lake palaeo data).
2. Our modern pollen data.
3. Our modern climate measurements.

The modern datasets includes the whole of North America and need to be filtered for the Eastern US so that the taxa are relevant to the those in Devil's Lake. We're first going to filter by longitude, then select by taxa so that we have a matching matrix of species between Devil's Lake palaeo-data and the modern surface samples from the NAMPD. We are going to keep all data East of 105°W, see @krause2019 and @williams2001.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Several columns hold information the MAT does not use, so keep the site
# identifier and the taxon counts only.
mod_pol_east <- mod_pol %>%
  filter(LONDD >= -105) %>% # keep sites east of 105 degrees west
  select(ID2, 14:147)       # ID2 plus the 134 taxon columns
```
:::


We will also filter the modern climate records by the same ID to match the modern pollen records.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_clim_filter <- mod_clim %>% 
  filter(ID2 %in% mod_pol_east$ID2)
```
:::


### Harmonising the taxon names {#sec-harmonisation}

Now the difficult part. The two datasets do not use the same taxon names, and they do not
identify pollen to the same level. Some examples of what stands in the way:

- Devil's Lake records *Picea*. The NAMPD splits spruce across three columns, `PICEAX`
  (undifferentiated), `PICGLAUC` (*P. glauca*) and `PICMARIA` (*P. mariana*).
- Devil's Lake records *Rhus*. The NAMPD has no *Rhus* column at all, but it does have
  `ANACARDI`, the family *Rhus* belongs to. The two names share no letters.
- Devil's Lake records *Sarcobatus vermiculatus* to species. The NAMPD only has the genus.
- The NAMPD's `RHAMNACEAE` column is not Rhamnaceae. Its metadata says it combines
  Rhamnaceae with Vitaceae.

Before the MAT can compare the two, every taxon has to mean the same thing on both sides.
**We have done that work already and saved the result as a table**, which you will load below.
It is worth knowing what went into it, because if you run this analysis on your own site you
will face the same kinds of decision.

#### The decisions behind the table

1. **What does the reference dataset's naming convention mean?** In the NAMPD a trailing `X`
   usually marks an undifferentiated taxon, so `PINUSX` is "Pinus - Pine undifferentiated".
   But `RUMEX` and `SALIX` end in `X` because the genus does, and most of the aggregate
   columns do not carry the suffix at all. The convention is documented in the workbook's
   `METADATA` sheet, and reading it is more reliable than inferring it from the codes.

2. **Which dataset is finer, and which way do you aggregate?** Neither, consistently. For
   *Picea* the NAMPD is finer, so its three columns are summed. For *Sarcobatus* Devil's Lake
   is finer, so the match is made at genus. For *Chenopodium* and Amaranthaceae, which the
   NAMPD combines in one column, two Devil's Lake taxa are summed together. The rule is to
   match at the coarser of the two levels and sum whichever side is finer.

3. **What happens when no name match is possible?** *Rhus* to Anacardiaceae, *Ilex* to
   Aquifoliaceae, *Morus* to Moraceae. These are botanical facts, not string similarities, and
   they have to be looked up and written down.

4. **What do you do with taxa that have no counterpart?** Devil's Lake records
   `Cannabaceae sensu stricto`, and the NAMPD has no Cannabaceae column, so those counts are
   discarded. `Angiospermae undiff. (herbs)` is unidentified herbaceous pollen with no
   equivalent, so it goes too. Both are decisions to record rather than problems to solve.

5. **Are the two datasets even counting the same kinds of thing?** This one matters most and is
   the easiest to miss. Devil's Lake was filtered to the ecological groups `UPHE` and `TRSH`,
   upland herbs plus trees and shrubs. The NAMPD's pollen sum also includes bryophyte and fern
   **spores**: *Sphagnum* alone is 4.2% of it. Comparing an assemblage of trees and herbs
   against one that is 4% peat moss inflates the dissimilarity for reasons that have nothing to
   do with vegetation. Matching the inclusion criteria is not a taxonomic judgement, it is a
   precondition.

An important point about all five: a name-matching algorithm cannot make any of these
decisions, and worse, it will not tell you that a decision was needed. The table below is the
output of a person going through the taxon lists and deciding, one at a time.

#### Loading and applying the table


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
harmonisation <- read_csv("./data/pollen-harmonisation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# One row per harmonised taxon. Each side's original names sit in a single
# plus-separated string, so the table stays short enough to read and check.
harmonisation %>%
  select(harmonised_taxon, devils_taxa, nampd_codes, decision) %>%
  head(10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   harmonised_taxon          devils_taxa               nampd_codes      decision
   <chr>                     <chr>                     <chr>            <chr>   
 1 Abies                     Abies                     ABIES            match   
 2 Acer                      Acer                      ACERX+ACNEGUNA+… sum     
 3 Alnus                     Alnus                     ALCRISPA+ALNUSX… sum     
 4 Ambrosia                  Ambrosia                  AMBROSIA         match   
 5 Amorpha-type              Amorpha-type              AMORPHA          match   
 6 Apiaceae                  Apiaceae                  APIACEAE         match   
 7 Artemisia                 Artemisia                 ARTEMISIA        match   
 8 Asteraceae undiff.        Asteraceae undiff.        ASTERCICHO+ASTE… sum     
 9 Betula                    Betula                    BETULA           match   
10 Caprifoliaceae sensu lato Caprifoliaceae sensu lato CAPRIFOLIA       match   
```


:::
:::


The `decision` column records what was done to each taxon: `match` for a straight
one-to-one, `sum` where several NAMPD columns roll up into one taxon, `coarsen` where Devil's
Lake was the finer of the two, `sum-both-sides` where taxa on both sides were combined, and
`drop` for the two taxa with no counterpart.

To use the table we expand those plus-separated lists into one row per original name, which is
what a join needs:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
harm_nampd <- harmonisation %>%
  filter(!is.na(nampd_codes)) %>%
  select(harmonised_taxon, nampd_codes) %>%
  separate_longer_delim(nampd_codes, delim = "+")

harm_devils <- harmonisation %>%
  filter(!is.na(harmonised_taxon)) %>%
  select(harmonised_taxon, devils_taxa) %>%
  separate_longer_delim(devils_taxa, delim = "+")

dim(harm_nampd)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 70  2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(harm_devils)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 49  2
```


:::
:::


Now the harmonisation itself, which is the same operation on both datasets: pivot to long
format, join the table on, then sum the counts within each harmonised taxon. The `inner_join`
is doing quiet but important work here, because any column absent from the table is dropped at
that step.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_pol_harm <- mod_pol_east %>%
  pivot_longer(-ID2, names_to = "nampd_codes", values_to = "count") %>%
  mutate(count = replace_na(count, 0)) %>%
  inner_join(harm_nampd, by = "nampd_codes") %>%   # unmatched columns dropped here
  group_by(ID2, harmonised_taxon) %>%
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = harmonised_taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0)

devils_harm <- devils_samples %>%
  inner_join(harm_devils, by = c("variablename" = "devils_taxa")) %>%
  group_by(age, harmonised_taxon) %>%
  summarise(count = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = harmonised_taxon, values_from = count, values_fill = 0)
```
:::


Two housekeeping steps before the analysis. The MAT needs the same taxa in the same order in
both matrices, and it needs the climate rows in the same order as the modern pollen rows.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
devils_ages <- devils_harm$age
mod_ids     <- mod_pol_harm$ID2

# The climate data must line up row for row with the modern pollen, and the
# MAT will not warn you if they do not. In this dataset they already match, but
# only because the 94 rows with a missing ID2 also have a missing longitude and
# are removed by the eastern filter. Do not rely on that: sort explicitly and
# then check.
mod_clim_filter <- mod_clim_filter %>%
  arrange(match(ID2, mod_ids))

stopifnot(identical(mod_clim_filter$ID2, mod_ids))

# the same taxa, in the same order, on both sides
shared       <- sort(intersect(names(mod_pol_harm), names(devils_harm)))
mod_pol_harm <- as.matrix(mod_pol_harm[shared])
devils_harm  <- as.matrix(devils_harm[shared])
```
:::


#### What the harmonisation cost

Harmonising always loses something, and it is worth reporting how much rather than hoping
nobody asks. Both matrices still hold counts at this point, so we can compare them against
what we started with.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(
  dataset       = c("Devil's Lake", "NAMPD"),
  taxa_before   = c(n_distinct(devils_samples$variablename), ncol(mod_pol_east) - 1),
  taxa_after    = length(shared),
  grains_before = c(sum(devils_samples$value), sum(mod_pol_east[-1], na.rm = TRUE)),
  grains_after  = c(sum(devils_harm), sum(mod_pol_harm))
) %>%
  mutate(pct_kept = round(100 * grains_after / grains_before, 2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  dataset      taxa_before taxa_after grains_before grains_after pct_kept
  <chr>              <dbl>      <int>         <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Devil's Lake          51         48        78378        78199      99.8
2 NAMPD                134         48      1456810.     1351550.     92.8
```


:::
:::


Two things stand out. Devil's Lake keeps almost all of its pollen, because only two of its
taxa had no counterpart. The NAMPD loses about 7%, most of it the spore and bryophyte columns
from decision 5 above, and the rest genuinely absent from Devil's Lake. The asymmetry is the
point: the reference dataset is richer than the core, and counts things nobody looked for at
Devil's Lake.

#### Converting to proportions

Only now do we convert to proportions, and the order matters. Squared chord distance is not
scale invariant, so if the rows no longer sum to one the two datasets are not comparable: a
fossil sample whose remaining taxa add up to 0.6 would look artificially far from every modern
sample. Dividing before dropping columns is a common and quiet way to get this wrong.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_pol_harm <- mod_pol_harm / rowSums(mod_pol_harm)
devils_harm  <- devils_harm  / rowSums(devils_harm)

# the data check from @sec-dissimilarity: both should be exactly 1
range(rowSums(mod_pol_harm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
range(rowSums(devils_harm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1 1
```


:::
:::


It is also worth seeing which taxa the aggregation changed most, since that is where the
harmonisation had the largest effect on the modern data:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
harmonisation %>%
  filter(decision %in% c("sum", "sum-both-sides")) %>%
  select(harmonised_taxon, nampd_codes) %>%
  mutate(n_columns = str_count(nampd_codes, fixed("+")) + 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_columns))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


::: {.callout-tip}
# Good practice tip
Whenever filtering or joining data it is good to check the dimensions before and after by using `dim()` to see if the results are what you expect. Some functions like `left_join()` or `full_join()` may run without error but produce unexpected results. It is also good to regularly use `rowSums()` to make sure you are using the correct data type (counts, proportions or percentages), and have not accidentally included age, depth, or ID columns if they should be excluded.
:::


## Cross-validation {#sec-crossvalid}

The Modern Analogue Technique needs the same set of taxa in the modern dataset and in the core data, which is what @sec-harmonisation produced: two matrices, `mod_pol_harm` and `devils_harm`, with identical columns and rows that sum to one.

Before reconstructing environmental variables from fossil pollen assemblages, we usually assess how MAT performs in the modern species assemblage. This step is usually referred to as calibration or cross-validation.

In cross-validation, a calibration function is trained on one portion of the modern species assemblages (calibration set) and applied to another portion of the modern species assemblages (validation set). These two datasets are thus mutually exclusive and, possibly, independent. To cross-validate MAT, we usually use a technique called $k$-fold cross-validation. In $k$-fold cross-validation the modern data set is split into $k$ mutually exclusive subsets. For each $k^{th}$ subset, the calibration dataset comprises all the samples not in $k$, while the samples in $k$ comprise the validation dataset. The simplest form of $k$-fold cross-validation is the leave-one-out (LOO) technique, in which just a single sample is removed and then all other samples are used to build a prediction for that sample. This procedure is then repeated for all samples. The `analogue` package uses leave-one-out cross-validation.

Standard metrics include root mean square error (RMSE) and $R^2$. Here, we’ll use the cross-validation tools built into the analogue package.

Note that the `palaeoSig` package, developed by Richard Telford, has additional functions that can test for significance relative to randomly generated variables with the same spatial structure as the environmental variable of interest. We won’t use this package in this chapter, but it’s useful for testing whether apparently strong cross-validation results are merely an artefact of spatial autocorrelation [@telford2005].

Now let's do the analysis! First is the cross validation of the modern datasets. Using the modern data, we’ll build a calibration dataset and run cross-validation analyses of the calibration dataset. If you portaled here and skipped the Data Wrangling in @sec-datawrangle, make sure you load in the pre-formatted data from @sec-background.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_jant <- data.matrix(mod_clim_filter$tjan)

modpoll_jant <- analogue::mat(mod_pol_harm, mod_jant, method = "SQchord")
```
:::

Much of the information in this chapter comes from @simpson2007, and we recommend @simpson2007 for the interpretation of the outputs. The MAT method shares similar considerations as calculating dissimilarity (@sec-dissimilarity). With some additional considerations regarding transfer functions:

- Time intervals and chronological uncertainties are not accounted for. The difference in time between successive samples often varies in palaeo-data.
- Time averaging is not taken into account, and each sample may contain a different time-span of ecological productivity.
- Squared chord distance is one of many distance measures available in `analogue`, and may not always be the most appropriate.

For deeper considerations of reconstructing temperatures using transfer functions see @telford2005.

## Novelty and palaeoclimatic reconstruction

For this part of the chapter, we’ll first assess the novelty of the fossil pollen assemblages at Devil’s Lake. We’ll then reconstruct past climates at Devil’s Lake, using the MAT. Here’s some demonstration code showing the kinds of analyses that can be done and plotted time series.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Minimum distance

Construct a time series of the minimum SCDs (novelty) for Devil’s Lake.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Predict temperatures from the fossil data and their modern analogue
devil_jant <- predict(modpoll_jant, devils_harm, k = 10)

par(mfrow = c(1,1))
devil_mindis <- minDC(devil_jant)
plot(devil_mindis, depths = devils_ages, quantiles = FALSE, xlab = "Age (yr BP)", ylab = "minSCD")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](no-analogue_files/figure-html/predictJanT-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Modern analogues

Construct a time series of the number of modern analogues found per fossil sample, using 0.25 as our no-analogue/analogue threshold. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
devil_cma <- analogue::cma(devil_jant, cutoff=0.25)

plot(x = devils_ages, y = devil_cma$n.analogs, type = "l", xlim= rev(range(devils_ages)), xlab = "Age (yr BP)", ylab = "Number of modern analogues")
```

## Exercises


1. In the summary output for JanT, which choice of k (number of analogues) produces the highest R2 and lowest RMSEP?
   1. Which samples at Devil’s Lake lack modern analogues?

2. Repeat the above analysis for TJul, PJul, GDD5, and MIPT. (GDD5 is growing degree days and is a measure of growing season length and strength; MIPT is an index of soil moisture availability).

3. Which variable has the best cross-validation statistics?
   1.  Which has the worst?

4. Given what you know about the climatic controls on plant distributions (and/or our ability to precisely quantify these variables), is the relative predictive skill for these different climatic variables surprising or unsurprising? Why?


5. Check the Devil’s Lake novelty curve against the pollen diagram for Devil’s Lake. What combinations of pollen taxa produce these no-analogue assemblages?

6. According to Webb(1986), what are two general hypotheses for why we might have these past mixtures of species with no modern analogue?

7. Why should one be dubious about the temperature reconstructions at Devil’s Lake for the high-novelty assemblages?

8. Even for the low-novelty assemblages, name two potentially important sources of uncertainty in MAT-based reconstructions of past climate from fossil pollen data.
   1. Conversely, based on our knowledge about the geographic climatic distributions of these taxa, why might one argue that these January temperature reconstructions are plausible?
